extracted.intended_audience: readers of colonial political criticism; historians and general literate public interested in West Indies governance
extracted.subtask_description: A critical essay evaluating Mr. Froude's representations of Trinidad, assessing governors, magistrates, policing, and claims about Negro felicity; exposes factual inaccuracies and concrete abuses. The piece uses case examples to judge administrative and judicial conduct under Crown Colony rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor fitness: strength of mind and firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: A governor should possess 'strength of mind whereof jobbers and peculators do stand in dread' and not be the kind of ruler who can be warped from 'softest commiseration' into devising 'the readiest method for slaughtering unarmed holiday-makers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites contrasting actions (protesting poor housing in 1883 vs sanctioning shooting in 1884) as evidence of lack of moral backbone; a worthy governor must resist external influences, oppose malfeasance, and act consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding caprice and vacillation in administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative leaders should not be 'a slave to red-tape, procrastination, and the caprices of pretentious colonialists' nor 'a daring schemer' exploiting resources for favourites; neither should they be 'an old woman, garbed in male attire, having an infirmity of purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer contrasts different successive governors to show that erratic character (procrastination, scheming, indecision) undermines good governance and fuels demands for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of advisers should be judicious and not ethnically narrow
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal governor 'should be allowed to choose his own advisers' but this does not mean advisers 'must be all pure-blooded Englishmen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisers should be chosen for competence and local knowledge rather than national origin; criticises any narrow interpretation that advisers must be metropolitan insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impute sordid motives without proof (avoid slander)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make culpatory statements against others 'without ability to prove them' is 'not criticism: it is slander.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accusations (e.g., that Reform leaders seek Crown salaries) must be supported by facts; disregarding or denying facts to sustain an allegation amounts to 'rank defamation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of ethnographic method / empirical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Superficial observation ('drives about the town and neighbourhood') is inadequate to learn 'what people were doing, how they were living, and what they were thinking about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author ridicules fleeting, surface-level inspection as incapable of producing faithful or detailed understanding; robust claims about a population require deeper, sustained investigation, not ephemeral glimpses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test abstract claims by concrete practical experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague hyperboles about 'Negro felicity' must be 'submitted to the test of practical experience, and the abstract government analysed in its concrete relations with the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of universal contentment should be evaluated against real-world indicators such as magistracy decisions, police practice, and documented abuses rather than rhetorical assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistracy's duty to shield the weak
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'immediate province of the MAGISTRACY' is the 'actual and direct interposition of the shielding authority' between man and man; magistrates should protect the weaker against the stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where stipendiary justices convert powers into 'an engine of systematic oppression' it negates the supposed protection offered by British rule; magistrates are judged by whether they fulfill this protective role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates must base judgments on impartial evidence, not preferential deference to police
rubrics_metrics.description: A magistrate who announces he will 'take the word of a constable in preference to the testimony of any one else' fails in impartial adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (Mr. R. D. Mayne) show that privileging constables—especially a partisan constabulary—leads to perjury-backed convictions and systemic injustice; fair courts require evaluation of all testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality and fairness in sentencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no proof, imposing harsh penalties (e.g., hard labour) or fines is scandalous; courts should not punish in the absence of proven guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited: woman almost sent to hard labour despite lack of proof but fined L2; husband and wife imprisoned after the larceny victim was discharged—these illustrate disproportionate and unjust punishment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police should ascertain facts before arresting
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper for a policeman to arrest someone without asking or waiting to hear the cause of the disturbance ('without asking or waiting to hear the cause ... he shouted "I see you are fighting: you are my prisoner!"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrests made without inquiry produce wrongful detentions and miscarriages of justice, as in the ironer's case; good policing requires fact-finding before enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court decisions must not be capricious or influenced by sympathy/pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates must avoid sudden caprice—e.g., reversing an acquittal by ordering an already-acquitted woman to hard labour because another defendant protested—demonstrating arbitrariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The L. B. case (dismissed then later sent to hard labour on the magistrate's whim) exemplifies how judicial caprice undermines rule of law and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial justice must protect vulnerable purchasers from fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal maxims like caveat emptor should not be perverted to reward deceit where the purchaser is demonstrably intended to be disadvantaged (e.g., selling an unsuitable larger cart to a man with only a donkey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magistrates must consider intent and practicality, not mechanically apply maxims to favour sharper parties; the donkey-cart case shows failure to protect the economically vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect longstanding cultural practices unless genuine danger exists; use proportionate remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hosein festival had, for nearly forty years, been allowed to procession without danger; sudden suppression and use of deadly force (shooting immigrants) was disproportionate and unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should weigh tradition and historical safety records before prohibiting cultural observances; proclamations should be clear about penalties and proportional responses—death was not listed in the prohibition yet was used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians and critics must avoid crass ignorance or deliberate malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that there was 'never any agitation for Reform in Trinidad before' are either 'crass ignorance or ... deliberate malice' when contradicted by record (e.g., 1843 elective constitution petition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate historical claims require consulting well-informed local sources and records; misstatement of the historical record undermines credibility and constitutes unfair criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local leaders' contributions and local knowledge are valuable qualifications for governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have 'borne the heat and the burden of the day'—enjoy local knowledge, confidence and respect—have rightful claim to the 'enjoyment of the fruits of their labours' and are important for efficient government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique argues that dismissing local reform leaders as motivated by salary ignores their practical value and sacrifices; evaluation of governance should value local competence and public service.
